query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In bulk HfNbTaTiZr, a multi‐scale simulation framework that explicitly incorporates point defects and 1 wt.% oxygen impurities – via ab initio–informed machine learning potentials – will predict the electrical conductivity with improved accuracy (within ±10% of experimental values) over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes compared to conventional models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr modeled as an ideal, single-phase, defect‐free crystal.
generation.intervention: Introduce modeled point defects and a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity into the simulation framework using ab initio–informed machine learning potentials.
generation.conditions: Applied across two regimes: a cryogenic regime (approximately 0–200 K) and an elevated temperature regime (approximately 300–1200 K), with comparisons between defect-free and oxygen-doped specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Presence of point defects and oxygen atoms that act as scattering centers, altering electron and phonon transport pathways.
generation.mechanism: Incorporating defect physics directly into the simulation captures additional scattering processes and impurity-induced localized states that modify conduction mechanisms, thereby bridging the gap between idealized models and experimental observations in both low and high temperature environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: The computational predictions will closely match experimental conductivity measurements for bulk HfNbTaTiZr in both temperature regimes, reducing errors beyond those inherent in analytical predictions limited to perfect crystals.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical approaches using perfect crystal approximations, which typically deviate by more than ±10% from experimental conductivity values when defects or oxygen impurities are present.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to remain valid within the tested temperature intervals (0–200 K and 300–1200 K); outside these regimes, additional quantum or diffusion effects might not be adequately captured by the current model.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative accuracy for the defect and impurity scattering mechanisms remains somewhat uncertain due to potential complexities in defect clustering and temperature-dependent dynamic effects that may not be fully resolved by the simulation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens both as near-perfect crystals and with a controlled addition of 1 wt.% oxygen. Use high-precision four-probe electrical conductivity measurements across the temperature ranges of 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Run corresponding multi-scale simulations incorporating explicit defect and impurity configurations. Compare the predicted conductivity values with the experimental benchmarks.
measurements: Microstructural analysis to confirm defect and oxygen distributions
Comparison of simulation-predicted scattering rates with indirect measurements (e.g., via Hall effect)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulated conductivity values deviate from the experimental measurements by more than ±10% in either the cryogenic or high-temperature regime for either the defect-free or 1 wt.% oxygen specimens, the hypothesis—that the new simulation method is more accurate than conventional analytical approaches—would be falsified.

These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
